title: An anniversary night
topic: Rotas, leave, and training versus service
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on a general medical rotation. On Thursday afternoon the rota coordinator messages you: a colleague has called in sick for Saturday night, and she asks whether you can cover.

Saturday is your wedding anniversary, and you have booked a dinner away for the night. You aren't rostered for that weekend.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Reply that you have plans for Saturday, and politely decline.
options.brief: You aren't rostered, and it's reasonable to protect important personal time.
options.detailed: You have no obligation to cover an unrostered shift, and time away from work matters for your wellbeing. A prompt, polite answer lets the coordinator look elsewhere straight away, so it ranks first.

options.text: Agree to cover, and cancel your plans.
options.brief: Generous, but at a real personal cost you aren't obliged to bear.
options.detailed: Covering would help the rota, and some doctors would choose to. But regularly sacrificing important personal time isn't sustainable, and you aren't obliged to. It ranks third: it is a choice, not a failing.

options.text: Leave the message unanswered until next week.
options.brief: Leaves the coordinator waiting for an answer she needs today.
options.detailed: Not replying wastes time the coordinator could spend finding cover. It's discourteous, but it doesn't directly put patients at risk, so it ranks above the last option.

options.text: Mention a colleague who said she'd like extra shifts.
options.detailed: Pointing to someone who wants extra work shows goodwill and may help her find cover quickly. It ranks second because a clear, prompt answer is what the coordinator needs most.

options.text: Agree to cover, but plan to leave the shift halfway through for your dinner.
options.brief: Creates an uncovered gap in a night shift.
options.detailed: Leaving part-way through a night shift would leave patients without a doctor. This is the only option that directly creates a risk to patient safety, so it is the least appropriate.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you can say no to extra work in a professional way, without creating risk for patients.
explanation.keyDetails: You aren't rostered. It's an important personal occasion. The coordinator needs an answer soon to find cover.
explanation.reasoning: [A] gives a clear, timely answer, and [D] adds a helpful suggestion. [B] is generous but not required, [C] wastes the coordinator's time, and [E] leaves patients without cover.
explanation.competing: Some would see [B] as the most professional response. The key respects your right to decline unrostered work, which is sustainable practice.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 4, looking after your own health and wellbeing.
